vignette:
She arrives precisely on time, her posture neat and professional, a laptop bag over one shoulder. She accounts for every detail of her day as if presenting a data model-timestamps, locations, probability. It takes several sessions before she stops treating the therapy hour like a weekly report to a supervisor.

That is how the story begins: in numbers. The day of the event was a Tuesday, 7:48 a.m., platform 4 of the central station. She was on her usual commute to the office, earbuds in, reviewing a scatter plot on her tablet. She does not remember hearing a scream. What she remembers is the wet sound, like a melon dropped from a height, and then the sudden absence of motion in her peripheral vision. The man on the tracks had been standing two paces to her left. She saw his arm jerk, a shove, then the seamless blur of the train. She did not see the other passenger's face. That part, she says, is missing from the data.

The police interviewed her. She answered questions with the same clarity she applies to a data-cleaning script: time, location, direction, number of people. She did not cry. She went to work that same afternoon, cleaned two datasets, attended a stand-up. She told no one. It was, in her mind, an outlier-a rare, improbable event that could be isolated and removed from the signal.

But the signal has decayed. Nine months later, she can no longer stand on any train platform. She takes a different, longer route to work, adding forty minutes each way, and always stands with her back against a wall. She avoids crowds, leaves meetings early, and has stopped taking the elevator at her office building. She has deleted all public transit apps from her phone. Her husband noticed she flinches when he approaches from behind. She told him it was nothing, a caffeine jitter.

At work, her colleagues praise her precision, but she feels the edges of her thinking fray. She runs the same regression three times, distrusting the output of her own mind. She cannot tolerate ambiguity. A missing value in a dataset sends a wave of heat through her chest; she imagines the gap as a person-shaped void, a zero that used to be a life. She has started flagging any data point that falls outside three standard deviations, even when it's valid. The outliers feel like warnings.

She sleeps poorly. She wakes at exactly 7:48 a.m., as if the day is already contaminated. She has not returned to the station. She avoids news articles about public violence, but fragments of her memory replay unbidden-the slick shine of the rail, the sudden dark shape under the train. She tells me she has analyzed every variable of that morning: the time, the weather, the passenger density. She believes if she just finds the pattern, she can retrofit a reason onto the randomness. But the model will not converge. There is no explanation for why the man was pushed, or why she was standing exactly there.

She holds herself still when she describes this, as though movement might crack something. Her husband has started to ask if she is okay. She says she is fine, but she has stopped cooking dinner together, stopped going to their neighborhood coffee shop. She works late, then sits in her car in the garage for fifteen minutes before going inside. She does not know why. She only knows that the world feels sharded, like a dataset with too many missing values, and she no longer trusts the code.
